claims.text: Governments pursue economic objectives such as employment, sustainable growth, price stability and a sustainable external economic position, alongside social aims such as improved living standards, fair opportunity, access to essential services and environmental protection. Objectives can conflict: a project creating employment may also damage a shared environment, while protection costs can limit some commercial activity. A business’s profit objective does not by itself show whether these wider aims are achieved. State the relevant outcome and parties rather than assume any increase in business output benefits everyone equally.

claims.text: Government may intervene because business choices can affect people who do not participate in the transaction, because workers or consumers may need protection, because competition and information may be imperfect, or because access to essential services and development objectives may not be met by commercial incentives alone. Intervention can use rules, incentives, public provision or information. It also uses resources and can create compliance costs or unintended effects, so explain the problem and whether the measure addresses it. A private profit is not proof of social harm, and the existence of regulation is not proof it works.

claims.text: Cost-benefit analysis is the valuation by a government agency of social and private costs and benefits resulting from a decision. Here the treatment is descriptive: identify the likely positive and negative effects, who bears or receives them, alternatives and important uncertainties. A business profit forecast covers only part of that wider assessment. A severe lasting effect may matter even when another benefit is easier to count. Avoid pretending that a list of benefits on one side automatically outweighs fewer but more serious harms.

claims.text: A descriptive appraisal separates private business effects from external community effects and compares realistic choices. Explain the mechanism, who is affected, whether the effect is temporary or lasting and how protection could alter it. A clean production option may preserve output while reducing neighbours’ harm, although it costs resources. Evidence can be incomplete, so give a conditional judgement rather than invent precise values for unmeasured consequences. Benefits and costs can be distributed unevenly; a gain to the business does not automatically compensate a resident.

claims.text: To apply the concepts, start with a stated decision and distinguish effects on the enterprise from effects on others. An external benefit is a gain to society beyond the business’s own return, such as other users gaining from a shared access improvement funded by a project. An external cost is harm or inconvenience borne by outsiders, such as disruption from deliveries. Describe alternatives and possible mitigation. A benefit elsewhere does not automatically remove a serious harm at the site; the resolution needs a reasoned balance and evidence.

claims.text: Government can protect against pollution through standards, monitoring, enforcement, information and incentives for cleaner methods. It can protect non-renewable resources through extraction limits, conditions, conservation and incentives to use materials efficiently. The measure must affect the actual mechanism and be capable of implementation. A rule without monitoring may change little; an excessive or poorly targeted burden can create costs without proportionate benefit. Distinguish reducing ongoing emissions from conserving a finite resource stock. Planting trees does not replace extracted mineral deposits.

claims.text: Social benefits are the gains to society resulting from a business decision, also known as external benefits in the syllabus. Distinguish wider benefits from the enterprise’s private revenue. Shared infrastructure improvement can benefit other users without becoming their purchase from the firm. Identify who gains and why; do not assume every project provides the same external benefit. Common social benefits of a new business or project are new jobs and lower local unemployment, tax revenue that pays for public services, better infrastructure such as roads, and other businesses moving into the area to supply it or its workers. Common social costs are air, water and noise pollution, loss of natural environment, extra pressure on water, electricity and roads, and congestion.
